title: How to read the claim store, and the graphics-card claims removed from it
body:
Stage B produced 2771 claims and no document saying what they are. This adds `docs/reading-the-claims.md`, written for whoever reads `data/claims.jsonl` next — most likely a model, with no memory of how the data got there.

**What the document covers.** Where every artifact lives and which of them are tracked (only `calibration/`; `data/` is gitignored by R21). The eight fields and the three closed vocabularies, with the note that `category` is the field carrying epistemic weight — a `tested` negative on `voltage_firmware_safety` is a measurement that a board does something harmful, a `reasoned` one is an inference from the design, and averaging them destroys the distinction. That `video_id` plus `timestamp_seconds` is a URL, so every claim is checkable in one click. A 40-claim random audit found **40 of 40 snippets present verbatim** in their source transcript — the property that makes this data evidence rather than assertion, and the reason the document insists a claim is never restated without its snippet and its link.

**Most of it is the four ways the data misleads a careless reader.** `board` is often a BRAND rather than a model, because the alias list carries brand-level canonicals, so grouping by it silently merges different products. Nothing has been aggregated or deduplicated, so counting positives counts sentences rather than opinions. Absence of claims is absence of coverage, not disagreement. And some claims are about graphics cards.

**`scripts/drop-gpu-claims.py` handles the last one.** The extraction prompt tells the model to skip claims about CPUs, chipsets and the industry; it never mentions GPUs, and Buildzoid reviews those too, so a GPU PCB breakdown produces well-formed claims about a product this project is not about. Fixing the prompt is the next extraction's job. This removes what the current corpus already holds.

**The rule is deliberately conservative, and the direction of its error is the point** — losing a real motherboard claim is worse than keeping a graphics-card one, which is the owner's explicit ruling in chat. Neither cheap signal works alone. Dropping by video throws away the real motherboard claims GPU videos contain, because Buildzoid discusses the board he is testing on. Dropping by board name misfires the other way: `MSI 970 Gaming Krait` is a motherboard, and `MSI`, `ASUS` and `ROG Strix` name both kinds of product. So three signals must agree: the video is about a card, the claim's own text talks about a card, and nothing in it names a chipset, socket, BIOS or motherboard family.

**It dropped 35 of 2771, and all 35 were read individually before applying it.** Every one names a graphics card, a GPU model number or card-specific hardware; none is a motherboard claim. About 90 claims from GPU-topic videos remain, most of them genuine motherboard remarks made during a GPU video, and the document says so rather than implying the corpus is now clean. The original store is kept at `data/claims.jsonl.bak`, and re-running the script finds nothing left to drop.

**Not tested by pytest.** It is a one-off data-maintenance script over a gitignored artifact, not product code, and `test-the-tests` skips this PR because nothing under `src/` changed. If the rule ever needs to run again on new extractions, it belongs in the prompt instead.

Ran locally: `plan-resolve.sh`, `escape-refs.sh`, `acceptance-criteria.sh`, ruff, `1954 passed`.
